Why Does Math Work? The Key Cut in a Closed Room
Yahweh's works are great, pondered by all those who delight in them. (Psalm 111:2)

Brothers and sisters, today we're going to talk about a subject that makes a lot of people want to nod off the moment they hear it: math. Don't close your eyes just yet! I promise there's no test today, you don't need a calculator, and I won't ask anyone to come up front and solve an equation.

Let me start with a question. Do you remember the one thing you muttered to yourself most often in math class back in school? I'm guessing many of us said it: "What's the point of learning this?" After all, you don't need to solve a system of linear equations to buy groceries, right?

Today I want to tell you something astonishing: math isn't just "useful." It's so useful that even the brightest scientists find it baffling. A person sits at a desk with a sheet of paper and a pen, works out some equations, and those equations turn out to reveal the deepest secrets of the universe. How on earth does that happen?
1. An Equation That Saw It Before the Telescope
In 1928, there was a British physicist named Paul Dirac. He had no giant laboratory and no super telescope. Using nothing but pen and paper, he wrote down an equation describing the electron.

But something strange happened. As he worked through the equation, an extra set of very odd "negative energy" solutions showed up. It's like doing the household accounts and finding at the end a mysterious extra sum of money in the ledger that you just can't reconcile.

Most people in that situation would probably say, "Oh well, I must have made a mistake somewhere. Let's erase it." But Dirac didn't erase it. He wrestled with it for several years, and in 1931 he boldly proposed an idea: the world must contain another kind of particle, a "positively charged electron."

Think about it: at that time, no one had ever seen such a particle. It's like someone holding up a treasure map and saying, "According to my calculations, there must be a cave behind that mountain, and there's treasure in the cave." Everyone was only half convinced.
And what happened? In 1932, the American physicist Carl Anderson actually found it in photographs of cosmic rays. It's what we now call the "positron."

What makes this so remarkable? An equation spoke a secret of nature before any telescope or laboratory could. It wasn't that someone saw the thing first and then wrote the formula. The formula came first, and only later did anyone see the thing.
Yahweh's works are great, pondered by all those who delight in them. (Psalm 111:2)

This verse says they are "pondered by all those who delight in them." Dirac's story tells us that God's works are not only great, they can also be pondered and investigated. The world he made is not a fog; it is a book that can be read. The more those who delight in his works investigate them, the more amazed they become.
2. Unreasonably Effective: The Locksmith and the Door
Dirac's story is not an isolated case. In 1960, the Nobel physicist Eugene Wigner wrote a famous essay with a long title: "The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences."

"Unreasonably effective" is a wonderful phrase. It means mathematics works so well that it's beyond reason. At the end of the essay, Wigner said something like this: the fitness of the language of mathematics for expressing the laws of physics is a wonderful gift which we neither understand nor deserve.
Did you catch that? A top scientist used the word "gift," and even said "we don't deserve it." That sounds almost like a testimony in church!
Let me give you three examples, and you'll see why he said that.

The first example I call "the math comes first, the use comes later." In 1854, the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, in his inaugural lecture, explored the geometry of curved space. He said space doesn't have to be flat and straight; it can curve from place to place. That lecture was published only after his death, in 1868. At the time this was pure mathematics, something mathematicians played with in their heads.

Then about sixty years later, in 1915, Einstein discovered that gravity can be understood as the curvature of spacetime. And what was the best tool for describing that curvature? Riemannian geometry! Riemann's mathematics became the language of general relativity.

The second example I call "imaginary numbers aren't imaginary." There's a number called i whose square is negative one. Sixteenth-century mathematicians found it absurd. How could a number multiplied by itself be negative? So they even named it an "imaginary" number, meaning a "fake number that doesn't exist."

Yet today, the fundamental equation of quantum mechanics, the Schrödinger equation, has this i written right there in plain sight. The "fake number" people once scorned turns out to be an indispensable ingredient for describing the world of the very small.

The third example I call "equations predict new things." James Clerk Maxwell wrote down the equations of electromagnetism, and those equations predicted that electromagnetic waves exist. In the late 1880s, Heinrich Hertz confirmed them in the laboratory. The phone in your hand and the radio in your car both depend on them today.
A Key Cut in a Closed Room

So what is this like? I love this picture: a mathematician is like a locksmith cutting keys in a closed room, who has never seen the door outside. He simply files away, cut by cut, following whatever seems reasonable and beautiful to him. But when the key is finished and he takes it out to try it, it fits the great door of the universe perfectly!
Would you call that a coincidence? Once is coincidence, twice is luck, but what about three times, four times, again and again?

In 1980, another mathematician, Richard Hamming, took up Wigner's question and kept thinking about it. He listed several possible explanations, for example: that we pick out the mathematics that happens to work, or that we look at the world through mathematical eyes, so all we see is mathematics. But in the end he frankly admitted that all these explanations together are still not enough.
3. Why Can We Read the Universe?
So why does mathematics work so well? To this day, scholars have no agreed answer. Broadly speaking there are three views, so let's look at them fairly.

The first is called Platonism. It holds that mathematical truths already exist, and that we "discover" mathematics rather than "invent" it. That makes a lot of sense, but it still needs to explain why these mathematical truths happen to govern the physical world.

The second is naturalism. It holds that the human brain learned to count through evolution, and that's why math is useful. That can explain why we can count one, two, three, but it struggles to explain why the advanced mathematics describing quanta and black holes is just as precise. Our ancestors hunting on the grasslands surely didn't need black holes, did they?

The third is the theistic view: the universe and the human mind come from the same rational Creator, so human reason can read the universe. I want to be honest: this is a philosophical inference, not an experimental result. But it leads us to a reasonable thought: if the author who wrote this great book of the universe is the same one who made our minds, then it isn't strange at all that we can read the book.
In the Beginning Was the Word
In fact, the Bible gave us a clue long ago. The Gospel of John opens with the Greek word for "the Word," Logos. Besides "word" or "speech," this word also carries the meaning of "reason."
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. (John 1:1)
All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made. (John 1:3)

Why isn't the universe a jumble of random numbers? Because it was made through the one who is the Word. Behind all things is a God who reasons and speaks, so all things have order and structure and can be understood.
In Proverbs chapter 8, Wisdom herself speaks, and says she was there when God created. The passage even contains a geometric picture.
When he established the heavens, I was there. When he set a circle on the surface of the deep, (Proverbs 8:27)
"Set a circle": doesn't that have a mathematical flavor? So when we used a compass as children to draw circles in our homework books, we were imitating the Creator!

So why does math work? It points to a beautiful answer: not because we are so great, but because God first put order into the universe, then made us in his image and gave us minds that can read his works.
Now let's see what this has to do with our everyday lives. I'd like to share three 321 principles with you.

First, the Bible is my standard. The universe has laws, and life has a standard too. An apple doesn't fall upward because it's in a bad mood, and the planets don't wander around on a whim. In the same way, God's Word is the law of our lives. When my thinking drifts off course, I don't edit God's Word to fit me; I let God's Word correct my thinking.

Second, change your mindset and you change your life. Many people tense up the moment they hear the word math, because in the past math meant tests, grades and pressure. But today we want to move from a human perspective to God's perspective: math is not just about grades; it's a tool for pondering God's works. When you see it that way, learning can become worship. A child doing homework, an adult balancing the books, can both be reading the book our Father wrote.

Third, humility overcomes pride. Being able to "read" the universe can easily make us proud, as if humanity were really something. But Wigner put it well: it's a gift, and we don't deserve it. We can read the universe not because we are great, but because God first put order into it. Let God be God, and let us be humble, grateful readers.

Here's an action for this week: write down one moment each day when you use math. Maybe it's counting change at the store, checking the time, or figuring out how long a drive will take. In that moment, softly say, "Lord, your works are great." You'll find that even the multiplication tables start to feel lovable.

Brothers and sisters, the multiplication tables and the Pythagorean theorem you learned were not invented by people to run the universe. The universe was already running according to that order; we only discovered it later.

The next time you see a formula, whether or not you understand it, you can remember: this is the handwriting the Word left in the universe. He is the God of wisdom and the faithful God. His world can be understood, and his heart can be known.
Let's be still for a moment and ask ourselves: Do I treat math as exam pressure, or as a window into the mind of the Creator?

Heavenly Father, thank you for making an orderly world that can be understood, and for giving me a mind that can think. Help me see your wisdom in my studies and my work. Whether I'm doing the accounts, studying or working, let it all become worship to you. In Jesus' name, Amen.
1. Dirac's equation announced the existence of the positron before any experiment did. What part of this story surprises you most, and why?
2. "Is mathematics invented or discovered?" Share your view, and talk about how "the Word" in John 1:1 helps us think about this question.
3. Which moment in your life that involves math could become a moment of worship where you say, "Lord, your works are great"? Share your specific action plan for this week.
Can Sunflowers Count? Fibonacci and an Honest Lesson
Yahweh, how many are your works! In wisdom have you made them all. The earth is full of your riches. (Psalm 104:24)
Friends, the next time you go to a flower market or walk past a field of sunflowers, I invite you to do something a little odd: crouch down and count the sunflower's seeds.
You might say, "Pastor, I buy flowers to arrange them, not to do math homework!" Don't worry. Today we're only counting spirals, not seeds.

Look closely at the head of a sunflower, and you'll see the seeds are arranged in two sets of spirals: one turning clockwise and one counterclockwise. If you're patient enough to count them, you'll often get 34 and 55, or 55 and 89. Pick up a pinecone, and its scales often form 8 and 13 spirals too.

34, 55, 89, 8, 13. These numbers look pretty random, don't they? But they actually come from the same family. Today we're going to get to know this family, and learn two lessons from it: one about God's wisdom, and one about honesty.
1. A String of Numbers, One Simple Rule

Do you see the pattern? Each number is the sum of the two before it. 1 plus 1 is 2, 1 plus 2 is 3, 2 plus 3 is 5, 3 plus 5 is 8. It's that simple; even an elementary school child can do it. This string of numbers is called the Fibonacci sequence.
The sunflower's 34, 55 and 89, and the pinecone's 8 and 13, are all in this sequence. It's as if flowers and pinecones had agreed ahead of time to choose numbers from the same family.
The Golden Ratio and the Golden Angle

There's another interesting thing about this sequence. If you divide two neighboring numbers, such as 89 divided by 55, the answer gets closer and closer to 1.618…. This number is called the golden ratio, and mathematicians represent it with the Greek letter φ.
Now take a full 360-degree turn and divide it into two parts according to the golden ratio. The smaller part is about 137.5 degrees. This angle is called the "golden angle."

As a plant grows at its tip, each time it produces a new seed or leaf bud, it is offset from the previous one by about 137.5 degrees. Points arranged this way pack most tightly without blocking each other. Keep placing them one after another, and Fibonacci-numbered spirals form naturally.
Placing Cups on a Round Table
That sounds a bit abstract, so let's try a thought experiment.

Suppose you're placing cups on a round table one at a time, and after each cup you turn the table by a fixed angle. What happens if you turn it 90 degrees each time? The cups stack up in four straight lines, leaving lots of empty space in between. What a waste of space.

But if you turn it by the golden angle each time, the cups spread evenly across the whole table, with nothing wasted. The sunflower is the host who is best at setting out cups; it arranges every seed just right.
Yahweh, how many are your works! In wisdom have you made them all. The earth is full of your riches. (Psalm 104:24)

The psalmist says, "In wisdom have you made them all." One tiny rule, turning by a fixed angle each time, brings both efficiency and beauty. That leads us to a reasonable thought: the Creator often uses the simplest laws to produce the richest beauty.
2. Full of Order, but Not Rigid
Someone might ask: plants don't have protractors, so how do they know to turn 137.5 degrees?

In 1992, two French physicists did a fascinating experiment. They dropped tiny magnetized droplets of oil one by one onto the center of a dish, letting the droplets repel each other and slowly drift outward. And guess what? The droplets arranged themselves into Fibonacci spirals!

This shows that the arrangement of leaves and seeds can arise from very simple physical rules: new growth pushes away from the old and takes its place in turn, and everything falls into place. As for exactly how this is regulated inside the plant, scientists are still studying it.

So does every sunflower dutifully follow the Fibonacci sequence? In 2016, a citizen science study examined 657 sunflowers. Of the 768 spiral counts recorded, about 74% were Fibonacci numbers; of the rest, some came from closely related sequences and some showed no clear pattern.

I love this result. It tells us that nature is full of order, but not mechanically rigid. The world God made isn't a factory assembly line where every item is identical; it has order, and it also has lively variety. It's just like us: every one of us is made in God's image, yet no two people look exactly alike.
God doesn't have to break the laws of nature to make himself known. The laws he established are themselves enough to make a single flower more beautiful than King Solomon's robes. Jesus said:

Why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They don't toil, neither do they spin, yet I tell you that even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these. (Matthew 6:28–29)

Notice that when Jesus told us to consider the flowers of the field, he didn't want us to count spirals. He wanted us to know that if the Father clothes a flower like this, how much more will he care for you?
God arranges every single seed so beautifully for one sunflower. Would he ignore your life? Would he not know about the things that worry you?

We are often like an anxious gardener who runs to the flowerpot every day, digs up the seed to see whether it has sprouted, buries it again, and digs it up again the next day. And the result? The poor seed is so disturbed it can never grow well. That's not how flowers grow. A flower rests quietly within the laws God has set, turning one small angle each day, and when the time comes, it blooms into a whole head of beauty.

Brothers and sisters, perhaps you're worried about your children's future, whether to stay in your job, your health, or your family's finances. Jesus didn't say these things don't matter. He said: your Father knows. Let's learn to grow quietly under God's care, like the flowers of the field.
3. An Honest Correction: The Overhyped Golden Ratio
Now that we're talking about the golden ratio, I need to give you an "honest correction."

You may have heard many claims: the Parthenon follows the golden ratio, the Mona Lisa follows the golden ratio, the proportions of the human body follow the golden ratio, and the nautilus shell follows the golden ratio. It's made to sound as though the golden ratio is the universe's master code, found everywhere.

The mathematician George Markowsky examined these claims and found that most of them rested on arbitrary measurements and strained data. It's like taking a ruler to a face: you can measure from anywhere to anywhere, and eventually you can always come up with the number you want.
Another mathematician, Clement Falbo, actually went to a museum and measured nautilus shells. The ratios came out between about 1.24 and 1.43, averaging about 1.33, not 1.618.
Friends, the nautilus shell is still beautiful, but it doesn't follow the golden ratio. And that's fine! God's glory isn't diminished one bit because a claim gets corrected.

I want to say something very important: people who fear God do not need exaggerated evidence. Sometimes we're so eager to speak well of God that we embellish what we've heard and make it sound more amazing than it really is. But when others check it and find it isn't true, it actually makes them doubt the gospel we proclaim.
God is the God of truth; he doesn't need us to "dress him up." The sunflower's real 74% honors God more than a made-up 100%, because it's true.
So what life lessons can we learn from the sunflower? I'd like to share three.

First, Jesus is my example. When Jesus saw a flower, he saw the Father's care. He didn't hurry past; he stopped to look and taught his disciples to look with him. We too need to learn to see the world through his eyes. The next time you pass a little flower by the road, don't rush to scroll your phone. Stop for a second, look, and think about the Father's care.

Second, give thanks in everything. Beauty is not an accident; it's a gift from the Father. The spirals on a flower, a pinecone or a pineapple are little surprises God has given us. Turn the beauty you see into thanksgiving, and there'll be a little less anxiety in your heart.

Third, honest witness. When we proclaim God's glory, we use true evidence, not exaggerated claims. This is moving from a human perspective to God's perspective. The human perspective says, "The more amazing the better, or people won't believe." God's perspective says, "The truth is enough, because I am the truth." At work, at home and when sharing the gospel, let's be witnesses whose words can be trusted.
This week's action: take a photo of a flower or pinecone, add Matthew 6:28–29, and send it to a friend who is anxious. Maybe that flower will be the greatest comfort they receive this week.
Brothers and sisters, one simple rule, offsetting by a golden angle each time, fills a whole flower head with beauty. God's wisdom is often like that: never showy, yet visible everywhere.

Find a flower, a pinecone or a pineapple, and count its spirals. As you count, slowly give thanks. Then ask yourself: What have I been anxious about lately? What can the flowers of the field teach me?

Heavenly Father, you clothe the flowers of the field, and you care for me too. Take away the anxiety in my heart, and let me grow quietly like a flower, giving the beauty back to you. Make me an honest witness, proclaiming your glory with words that are true. In Jesus' name, Amen.
1. Hearing that sunflowers form beautiful spirals using one simple "golden angle" rule, what new insight do you have into God's wisdom?
2. The nautilus shell doesn't follow the golden ratio. What does this "honest correction" remind you of? Have you ever exaggerated a claim to make your faith sound more convincing?
3. What have you been anxious about lately? After reading Matthew 6:28–29, how do you want to hand that worry over to the Father?
Unchanging Within Change: The Beauty of Symmetry in a Snowflake
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow. (James 1:17)
Brothers and sisters, what's the most unusual New Year's gift you've ever received? A red envelope? A holiday feast? A new set of clothes?
In 1611, an astronomer received... no, wait, he gave a very unusual New Year's gift. His name was Johannes Kepler. He wrote a little book for a friend, titled On the Six-Cornered Snowflake.

Imagine a friend giving you a book for the New Year, and when you open it, it's all about why snowflakes have six sides. Wouldn't you think your friend was a bit odd? But Kepler asked a very good question: why are snowflakes always six-sided, never five-sided or seven-sided?

Every snowflake has six points. Some look like stars, some like ferns, some like tiny hexagonal plates. Their shapes vary endlessly, yet they all come in sixes. Today, starting from this tiny snowflake, we'll talk about a beautiful mathematical idea: symmetry.
Have you entered the treasuries of the snow, or have you seen the treasures of the hail, (Job 38:22)
When God asked Job this question, it was as if he were saying, "Job, do you really understand snow?" Today, let's step into God's storehouse of snow together and take a look.
1. What Is Symmetry? The Secret of the Snowflake
Turn It, and It's Still the Same

How do mathematicians define symmetry? It's actually very simple: if something goes through some change, such as a rotation, a flip or a shift, and afterward it looks exactly the same, that's called symmetry.

Take a snowflake. Turn it 60 degrees, and it looks just as it did before. Turn it another 60 degrees, and it's still the same. After six turns, it's right back where it started. That's the snowflake's six-fold symmetry.

So what's the answer to Kepler's question? It turns out that when water molecules freeze, they line up in a hexagonal lattice. So from the very beginning, a snowflake grows in a six-sided form. Its basic shape is set by the arrangement of its molecules.

Then why are the fine branches of every snowflake different? That depends on the temperature and humidity it passes through as it falls from the sky. The physicist Kenneth Libbrecht has studied snowflakes for decades and has described these growth processes in detail.

It's like a group of children who all grow up in the same home, with the same house rules and the same parents, so deep down they all have the "family look." But each child walks a different path, and each develops a distinct personality.

The church is like that too. We have the same Father God, the same Bible and the same Holy Spirit, so we all bear "the likeness of Christ." But every brother and sister has walked a different road. Some have been through suffering, some through good times, so everyone's testimony is different. Being different isn't a problem; that's exactly God's richness.

What is symmetry like? It's like a kaleidoscope. You put in a few colored fragments, let the mirrors reflect them, and a complete, harmonious pattern appears. One simple rule, repeated in every direction, produces beauty.
2. The Rules of Crystals, and the Quasicrystal That Broke Them
When mathematicians studied crystals, they found a rule: any crystal that repeats regularly allows only two-, three-, four- and six-fold rotational symmetry. Five-fold symmetry is impossible.

Why? Think of tiling a floor. Squares can cover it completely, and so can equilateral triangles and regular hexagons; that's how a honeycomb works. But if you try to tile a floor with regular pentagons, no matter how you arrange them, you'll always leave gaps.
Yet in 1984, research was published showing an alloy with five-fold symmetry, and it did not repeat regularly. This kind of material later came to be called a "quasicrystal."

At first many people doubted the discovery. They said, "Impossible! The textbooks say there can't be five-fold symmetry!" But the truth is the truth, and the discovery later won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

I love this story. It tells us that God's creation is richer than our textbooks. Just when we think we've figured out all the rules, God still has surprises hidden away, waiting for humble people to discover them. It also reminds us that scientists and Christians alike need a heart that is willing to be corrected and willing to learn.
3. Noether's Theorem: Because It Doesn't Change, It's Conserved
Next I want to introduce a very profound theorem. In 1918, the German mathematician Emmy Noether proved that every continuous symmetry of the laws of nature corresponds to a conservation law.
That sounds a bit heavy, so let me break it into three sentences we can all understand.
First, if the laws don't change over time, energy is conserved. In other words, the laws of physics today are the same as yesterday, so energy doesn't appear out of nowhere or vanish into thin air.
Second, if the laws don't change from place to place, momentum is conserved. A law that holds in Taipei also holds in Kuala Lumpur.
Third, if the laws don't change with direction, angular momentum is conserved. Whether you face east or west, the laws are the same.
Friends, what is the heart of symmetry? It can be put in a few words: "something unchanging within change." The snowflake turns, but its shape doesn't change; time passes, but the laws don't change.

Because the laws of the universe are the same yesterday and today, energy is conserved and the sun rises as usual. In fact, that the laws of physics are the same everywhere in time and space is a precondition for doing science at all. If the laws changed every day, the experiments scientists do today wouldn't count tomorrow.

So what does this "unchangingness" point to? It leads us to a reasonable thought: it points to a faithful, unchanging Lawgiver. This is a philosophical inference, but the Bible told us clearly long ago that God himself is the one who never changes.
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow. (James 1:17)
For I, Yahweh, don't change; therefore you, sons of Jacob, are not consumed. (Malachi 3:6)

Notice this phrase in Malachi: "therefore you, sons of Jacob, are not consumed." Why did the Israelites fall again and again, yet were not destroyed? Not because they were good enough, but because God does not change.

Our moods change, our circumstances change, the stock market changes, the weather changes, even how people treat us changes. But God's love and promises do not change. This is the most solid foundation for our faith.

I remember riding a merry-go-round as a child. The horses go up and down, the scenery keeps spinning, and if you ride long enough you get dizzy. But if you fix your eyes on the pole in the very center, you won't get dizzy, because that pole doesn't move. Life is like a merry-go-round too: work is spinning, family is spinning, our health is spinning, the world's news is spinning. We need a pole that doesn't move, and that is our faithful God.

Sometimes we wonder, "Has God stopped loving me?" because we've prayed for a long time and nothing has changed. But remember: a snowflake turned sixty degrees still looks just as it did before. Your situation may have turned all the way around, but God's love is still just as it was. Yesterday, today and tomorrow, he keeps his covenant and shows you steadfast love.
So how does this snowflake come into our lives? I'd like to share three 321 principles.

First, Jesus is my example. Jesus' love for his disciples never wavered. Peter was impulsive, Thomas doubted, the disciples often didn't understand what was going on, but Jesus didn't change his love because of it. I want to learn from him and live out faithfulness in my relationships. When I say I'll do something, I do it; when I make a promise, I keep it.

Second, life first, then relationships. Because a snowflake has an unchanging six-sided core, it never loses its shape no matter how it grows on the outside. Our lives are the same: there needs to be an unchanging core inside, and then our relationships will be stable. Where does that core come from? From drawing near to God first, every day. First root your life in the unchanging God, and then face the people and things that do change.

Third, 920, the fruit of the Spirit. One of the fruits the Holy Spirit produces is "faithfulness." By nature we are unsteady people: passionate today, cold tomorrow; promising today, forgetting tomorrow. But the Holy Spirit can shape our unsteady selves into steady people.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. (Galatians 5:22–23)

This week's action: think of a small promise you made to someone but haven't yet kept. Maybe you promised your child you'd play with them, maybe you told a friend you'd call back, maybe you promised God you'd read the Bible every day. This week, follow through on it.
Brothers and sisters, when it rains or snows, look out the window, or find a magnified photo of a snowflake online. Let its delicate detail quiet your heart.
Every snowflake is softly saying, "Something unchanging within change." And behind all the changes stands the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation, nor turning shadow.
Let's quietly reflect: What is changing in my life right now? Which of God's unchanging promises can I hold on to tightly?

Faithful Father, with you there is no variation or turning shadow. In changing days, be my anchor, and make me a person who keeps my word, faithful and dependable. May the Holy Spirit produce the fruit of faithfulness in me, so that at home, at work and in the church I reflect your faithfulness. In Jesus' name, Amen.
1. The snowflake's "unchanging within change" brings to mind which things in your life are changing right now? And which of God's promises do not change?
2. The discovery of quasicrystals was doubted at first but later won a Nobel Prize. What does this story remind us about facing new knowledge and being corrected?
3. Do you have a promise you made but haven't kept yet? Share how you plan to keep it this week, and ask your group to pray for you.
The Most Beautiful Equation: Five Strangers Who Turned Out to Be Family
One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after: that I may dwell in Yahweh's house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh's beauty, and to inquire in his temple. (Psalm 27:4)
Brothers and sisters, if I asked you, "What do you think is the most beautiful thing in the world?" you might say a sunset, the ocean, a newborn baby, or a photo of your spouse when they were young.
But if you ask mathematicians, many of them will give you a strange answer: "The most beautiful thing is an equation."

You might be thinking, "An equation? What's beautiful about an equation? Equations just give me a headache." Hang on. Today I'm going to introduce you to the equation many mathematicians call "the most beautiful." I promise that even if you don't understand it at all, you'll still be able to feel its beauty.
The equation is just one short line. Read aloud, it goes like this: e to the power of iπ, plus 1, equals 0.

That's it; there's nothing more. It links the five most fundamental numbers in mathematics (0, 1, π, e and i) using addition, multiplication, an exponent and a single equals sign. Not one symbol too many, not one too few.
1. Five Main Characters from Every Corner
Let me introduce these five main characters as they come on stage.
The first is 0. It stands for nothing at all, and it's the starting point of addition. Add 0 to any number, and it stays the same.
The second is 1. It's where all counting begins, and it's the starting point of multiplication. Multiply any number by 1, and it stays the same too.

The third is π, about 3.14159. It's the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. Whether it's a coin or a large pizza, the circumference divided by the diameter is always π. It comes from geometry.
The fourth is e, about 2.71828. It describes continuous growth, such as compound interest at the bank, or the decay of matter. It comes from calculus.
The fifth is i, the "imaginary unit" whose square is negative one. It comes from algebra.

Did you notice? These five numbers come from completely different backgrounds: one from arithmetic, one from geometry, one from calculus, one from algebra. Normally each is busy in its own field, and they seem to have nothing to do with one another.

It's like five people from different countries, speaking different languages, who don't know each other at all. One day they happen to sit at the same dinner table, get to talking, pull out their family trees to compare, and discover, "Oh my, we're actually one family!"
That's what's so astonishing about this equation: the five numbers in mathematics that seem least related to each other are holding hands in a single line.

Here's another picture. You go to a wedding and see the groom's relatives, the bride's friends, coworkers from the office and brothers and sisters from church, people who would never normally sit together. But on that day, because of the same couple, everyone sits in the same banquet hall and raises a glass together. What brought them together? That shared center.
In Euler's identity, the five numbers also have a shared center: that little equals sign. It holds everything in balance, and in the end it all equals 0, clean and tidy, with nothing left over.
2. Mathematicians Are Moved by Beauty Too
Where does this equation come from? It comes from a bigger formula called Euler's formula: e to the power of ix equals cos x plus i times sin x.

In 1748, the mathematician Leonhard Euler set out this relationship systematically in his work Introduction to the Analysis of the Infinite. Just replace x with π, and you get the most beautiful equation. But I also need to tell you honestly that historians note it is still uncertain whether Euler himself ever wrote this exact one-line form.
Do mathematicians really find it beautiful? In 1990, The Mathematical Intelligencer published a reader poll, and this equation came in first; it was voted the most beautiful theorem.

Even more interesting is a study from 2014. Researchers at University College London asked 15 mathematicians to rate the beauty of 60 formulas while their brains were being scanned. Euler's identity was most consistently rated the most beautiful.

The study also found that when mathematicians experience mathematical beauty, the area of the brain that becomes active is the same as when they enjoy the beauty of music and art. Of course, the study's sample was small, and more research is needed. But at least it shows us that, to a mathematician, a good formula is like a good poem, a good painting or a good piece of music.

Friends, isn't that wonderful? God not only made a universe that can be described with mathematics; he also made people who can be moved by the beauty of mathematics. That mathematical beauty and truth so often go together, and that humans can perceive this beauty, points to a Creator who is himself beautiful and good. This is a philosophical inference, but it's a warm one.
At this point I'd like to tell you a little more about Euler himself. He was one of the most prolific mathematicians in history, and also a devout Christian.
In 1747 he published a small book defending divine revelation, answering the objections of the freethinkers of his day. In his later years Euler was almost blind, but he kept on writing prolifically.

Just imagine: an old man whose eyes could hardly see, yet whose heart could see the beauty of mathematics and the beauty of God. His eyes grew dim, but his heart was full of light. Isn't that inspiring?

Some people think faith and scholarship are opposed: if you want to be smart, you can't believe in God; if you want to believe in God, you'd better not think too hard. Euler's life shows us that isn't true. He was a top mathematician and a devout Christian, and he was willing to stand up and speak for God's revelation.

Brothers and sisters, you don't have to be a mathematician, but in your own field you can be a "Euler" too. Whether you're a teacher, an engineer, an accountant, a nurse or a homemaker, you can use your intelligence and talents as a channel for knowing God and glorifying him.
3. All Things Held Together in Christ
Euler's identity tells us something: the different branches of mathematics seem independent of each other, yet deep down they are connected.
The Bible tells us something similar: all things are held together in Christ.
He is before all things, and in him all things are held together. (Colossians 1:17)
Five numbers found a home in one equation. All things in the universe, too, find their center and meaning in Christ.

This makes me think of our own lives. We often cut life into several pieces: this is work, that's family, this is ministry at church, that's personal hobbies. Each piece seems to fight for time, and they clash with each other, leaving us tired and scattered.

Just like those five numbers: if they stayed scattered in their own fields, they would never know how they relate to each other. But when they are put together into that equation, they become one harmonious whole.

Our lives also need a "formula" that connects all the scattered pieces. That formula isn't a method; it's a person, Jesus Christ. When he becomes the center, work, family and ministry no longer fight each other; together they become worship to him.
David was a king. He had wealth, power and fame. But what was his greatest desire in life?
One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after: that I may dwell in Yahweh's house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh's beauty, and to inquire in his temple. (Psalm 27:4)

Not to gain something, but to behold the beauty of God. The beauty of mathematics is only a small window; beyond it is the beauty of God himself. Euler's identity is beautiful, but it's only a faint reflection of God's beauty.
Now let's take this equation into our lives. I've chosen three 321 principles.

First, let Jesus reign. Only when every part of life is under his lordship can it come together in harmony as one. If work reigns, the family suffers; if our emotions reign, our relationships get hurt. Only when Jesus reigns does every part find its proper place.

Second, with the heart, by the Spirit. Beauty is not only analyzed with the mind; it is appreciated with the heart. You don't need to be able to solve Euler's formula to appreciate its simplicity, just as you don't need to know how to compose music to be moved by a hymn. Let the Holy Spirit open our hearts, so that in appreciating we worship.

Third, give thanks in everything, and give the glory to Jesus. This is also at the core of 321: let Jesus receive all the glory. Every time you see beauty, whether it's an equation, a sunset or a child's smile, say, "This is the Lord's beauty."

The Hotel That Never Fills Up: Finite People and an Infinite God

He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can't find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end. (Ecclesiastes 3:11)

Brothers and sisters, have you ever had this experience? You're traveling, you arrive late at night, you walk up to the hotel front desk, and the clerk says apologetically, "I'm sorry, we're fully booked tonight." You feel exhausted and discouraged all at once.

Today I want to introduce you to a very special hotel. It has infinitely many rooms: Room 1, Room 2, Room 3… the numbers go on forever, and there's never a last room. And tonight, every single room is occupied.
Just then, another weary traveler arrives. Can he still get a room?

Common sense says full is full, right? But the owner of this hotel is clever. He picks up the intercom and says, "Dear guests, sorry for the trouble, but would the guest in Room 1 please move to Room 2, the guest in Room 2 move to Room 3, and everyone move down one room."
Because there are infinitely many rooms, everyone has a next room to move into. Once they've all moved, Room 1 is empty! The new guest happily checks in.
This thought experiment is called "Hilbert's Hotel." It tells us something: infinity plays by completely different rules from the finite world we know.
Great is Yahweh, and greatly to be praised! His greatness is unsearchable. (Psalm 145:3)
Today, let's talk about "infinity," and about the God whose greatness is unsearchable.
1. How Do You Compare Infinities? The Dance-Partner Method
In the nineteenth century there was a German mathematician named Georg Cantor. He asked a question that sounds very simple: given two collections of things, how can you tell which has more?
You might say, "Just count them." But what if both collections are infinite and you can never finish counting?
Cantor's answer was "one-to-one pairing." If everything can be paired off, the two are the same size.

Let's picture a dance. There's a group of boys and a group of girls. You don't need to count them one by one; you just call out, "Everyone find a partner!" If every boy takes the hand of a girl, and every girl takes the hand of a boy, with no one left over, then the two sides have the same number. Even if there are too many people to count, it doesn't matter.
Using this method, Cantor arrived at some wonderful results.
First, there are as many even numbers as natural numbers. How do you pair them? Pair 1 with 2, 2 with 4, 3 with 6, and keep going. The pairing never runs out, and no one is left over.

Friends, the even numbers are obviously only half of the natural numbers, so how can there be just as many? That's a feature of infinity: a part can be as large as the whole. In the finite world this is impossible; in the infinite world it's true.

Second, there are just as many fractions. The fractions look densely packed, far more numerous than the natural numbers, but Cantor discovered that all the fractions can also be lined up in a single list and paired one-to-one with the natural numbers.
2. Above Every Infinity, a Larger Infinity
By now you might think, "So all infinities must be the same size, right?"

Cantor went on to prove something even more astonishing: no matter how you list all the real numbers on the number line, you will always miss some, so they cannot be paired one-to-one with the natural numbers. In other words, the infinity of the real numbers is larger than the infinity of the natural numbers!

He first proved this in 1874, and in 1891 he presented his famous "diagonal argument." It's as if, at the dance, no matter how the host arranges things, someone on the real-number side can never find a partner.
And that's not all. Cantor also proved that for any set, the set made up of all its subsets is always larger.

What does that mean? It means that given any infinity, you can always build a larger infinity; and from that larger one, you can build one larger still. Above every infinity there is a larger infinity, like a never-ending staircase whose top you can never reach.

At first Cantor's theory met fierce opposition from some mathematicians. But in 1926 the mathematician David Hilbert made a famous declaration: "No one shall expel us from the paradise that Cantor has created."
A theory that was opposed later became a paradise in mathematicians' eyes. This reminds us that truth sometimes needs time before people can see it.

Friends, is your head spinning a little by now? That's fine; being dizzy is normal! It means we've run into something far bigger than ourselves. Our minds are finite, and trying to think about infinity with a finite mind is like trying to hold the whole Pacific Ocean in a little teacup. Of course it won't fit.

But here's the wonder: although we can't contain it, we can think about it, talk about it, and even prove things about it. A little teacup somehow knows how big the Pacific is, and even knows there are greater oceans beyond it. That in itself is something very unusual.
3. God's Infinity Is Not the Biggest Number

Many people don't know that Cantor was a devout Lutheran. He made a very important distinction: mathematical infinities he called "transfinite numbers," but there is another kind, the "absolute infinite," which belongs to God alone. He held that this absolute infinite could never be fully grasped by any mathematics.

He also corresponded with Catholic theologians, and even wrote to Pope Leo XIII, discussing the relationship between infinity and theology. Here was a mathematician engaged in the most abstract research, and his heart was thinking about God.

Here we need to beware of a common misunderstanding: God's infinity is not "the biggest number." If God were only the biggest number, Cantor's staircase tells us you could always build a bigger one, and then God wouldn't be God.
Mathematical infinity is a created concept, something people explore in thought; God himself is the source of the infinite. His wisdom, power and love are all beyond measure.
Great is our Lord, and mighty in power. His understanding is infinite. (Psalm 147:5)
But will God in very deed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens can't contain you; how much less this house that I have built! (1 Kings 8:27)
Solomon built the temple, yet he clearly admitted that heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain God, so how could a single house?
The Infinite God Enters the Finite
And yet this is the most wonderful thing about the gospel: this infinite God was willing to enter the finite. The Word became flesh and lived among us.

Even a hotel with infinitely many rooms can squeeze in one more guest, but what God did is more wonderful still: he himself came into this world, and when he was born there was no room for him. He left infinite glory to give us an eternal home.
More than that, he has set "eternity" in our hearts.

He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can't find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end. (Ecclesiastes 3:11)

That's why we're so often dissatisfied. We buy a new phone and are happy for three days; we get a promotion and are excited for a month. Then our hearts feel empty again. Because God has set "eternity" in our hearts, temporary things can't fill it.

It's like an infinitely large room that you keep filling with furniture. You move in a sofa, and it's still empty. You move in a TV, and it's still empty. You move in a whole set of designer goods, and it's as empty as ever. The problem isn't that the furniture isn't good enough; it's that this room was made for the infinite God. Only when he moves in will the room be full.
So that emptiness in your heart that you can't quite put into words isn't a flaw in you; it's a sign. It's reminding you that you were made for eternity, that you were made for God.

That finite humans can think about and prove things about infinity shows that a longing and capacity reaching beyond the finite has been placed in the human heart. It leads us to a reasonable thought: it points to the eternal, infinite God.
I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End. (Revelation 22:13)
Stepping out of the infinite hotel, how should we live? I'll share three 321 principles.

First, from the temporary to the eternal. Weigh today's choices with eternity in view, and ask: What really matters? Many of the things that make us argue, lose sleep and worry turn out to be very, very small when measured on the ruler of eternity.

Second, humility overcomes pride. Brilliant as Cantor was, he admitted there is an infinity that mathematics cannot grasp. However clever we are, we are still finite. Admitting our limits is not shameful; it's wise. When we let God be God, we can rest.

Third, people matter more than tasks. People have eternal souls, but tasks all pass away. Reports pass away, houses grow old, grades are forgotten, but every person around you is eternal. So spend a little more time on people.

Turn my eyes from the temporary to the eternal, let me pursue you all my life, and let me invest my time and love in people who are eternal. In Jesus' name, Amen.

The Universe on a T-Shirt: Simple Laws and the Summary of Love
The whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments. (Matthew 22:40)

Brothers and sisters, do you have one of those really, really thick instruction manuals at home? You buy a washing machine and it comes with a fifty-page booklet; you buy a new phone and the manual is thicker than a novel. Honestly, most of us have never read one all the way through, right?

We often assume that the more important and complex something is, the thicker its manual should be. So the instruction manual for the whole universe ought to fill an entire library, wouldn't you think?
But here's the wonder: the deepest laws of the universe turn out to be very short.
F equals m a. Three letters that describe motion, from an apple falling to a rocket lifting off.
E equals m c squared. Five symbols that show mass and energy can turn into each other; this is how the sun shines.
All of electromagnetism, including electricity, magnetism, light and radio, can be written as four equations, short enough to print on a T-shirt.
Friends, you can wear the universe's instruction manual! Today let's talk about why the deepest laws of the universe are often the shortest to write.

The first example is Newton's second law. In 1687 Isaac Newton set out his laws of motion in his work, the Principia. Interestingly, the familiar form we know today, "F equals m a," was put together later by other mathematicians.

This tells us that truth often needs generation after generation to organize and refine it before it becomes so clean and crisp. It's like a piece of uncut jade: only after polishing does its brilliance show.

The second example is James Clerk Maxwell. In 1865 he published his theory of the electromagnetic field. Originally there were about twenty equations, which looked pretty intimidating. Later scholars rewrote them using vectors and condensed them into today's four.

Even more impressive, these equations calculated the speed of electromagnetic waves, and it came out exactly equal to the speed of light! This revealed a great secret: light is an electromagnetic wave.
Think about it: humanity had looked at light for thousands of years without knowing what it was. The answer was hidden in a few equations, and once they were worked out, suddenly it all made sense.

It's a bit like playing "spot the difference." You stare at two pictures for ages and can't find a thing; then someone points lightly and you exclaim, "There it is!" The answer was there all along, just waiting to be seen.
The third example is Albert Einstein. In 1905, in a paper only three pages long, he derived the mass–energy relation, E equals m c squared.
Three pages! Many of us write reports longer than that. Yet those three pages explained why the sun shines.
So the next time you're out walking in the sunshine, think about this: behind the warmth on your face is such a short line of symbols.

Friends, we often assume impressive things must be complicated. But true masters can often make complicated things simple. A good teacher can explain a difficult idea in one sentence; a good chef can make the most delicious dish from the simplest ingredients. The laws of the universe seem to come from a master like that.

What is a good law like? It's like a good map. A good map doesn't draw every tree and every rock; otherwise it would be as big as the land itself and completely useless. A good map gathers countless details into a few lines without distorting them. The more skilled the mapmaker, the simpler the map.
The laws of the universe are a map like that. Countless phenomena are gathered into a few short lines. That leads us to a reasonable thought: the one who drew this map is a wise and orderly Lawgiver.

Friends, however well a map is drawn, it can't walk by itself; its value lies in getting you to your destination. The map of the universe's laws is the same. It isn't the destination; it's a signpost pointing to the one who drew the map.
2. Beauty Is a Clue, Not the Judge

When it comes to the beauty of simplicity, the physicist Paul Dirac had a view. He said that if someone works from the viewpoint of seeking beauty in their equations, and has really sound insight, they are on a sure line of progress. His own electron equation was a case in point.

But I also need to tell you very honestly that some physicists warn that beauty is not the same as truth. Some very elegant theories have still not found experimental support today. Whether "mathematical beauty" is a reliable clue to truth is still debated among physicists.
So what's a more balanced view? Beauty can be a clue, but in the end experiment must decide.

This is an important reminder for our life of faith too. A sermon that sounds moving, a line that sounds lovely, an idea that feels right, isn't necessarily correct. Beauty can draw us in, but the final judge is God's Word. Just like the Bereans, who heard Paul preach and still examined the Scriptures every day to see whether it was true.
3. God's Law for People Has a Simple Summary Too
Jesus Condensed the Old Testament into Two Sentences
The laws of the universe are simple, and the law God gave people also has a simple core.

Once, someone came to Jesus and asked, "Which is the greatest commandment in the law?" The Old Testament has so many regulations and so many words from the prophets that most people would probably have written a long list. But Jesus condensed the whole Old Testament into two sentences:

“‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ This is the first and great commandment. A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ The whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments.” (Matthew 22:37–40)
Friends, isn't this the "F equals m a" of the spiritual world? All the teaching can be gathered up into "love God, love people."

I love this picture: the person asking may have expected a long list, but Jesus handed him a little card. A list keeps people busy ticking boxes; a summary brings people back to the heart. What Jesus cares about isn't just how many items you've completed, but whether your heart is aligned toward God and toward people.
Love doesn't harm a neighbor. Love therefore is the fulfillment of the law. (Romans 13:10)
But let me remind you of one thing: simple does not mean easy.

F equals m a is just one line, but engineers spend a lifetime applying it to build bridges, cars and rockets. "Love God, love people" is just two sentences, and we too must spend a lifetime living it out.

Remembering it is easy; a three-year-old can recite it. Living it out is a lifelong lesson. It's like a student who has memorized F equals m a perfectly but can't solve a single word problem on the exam. Many Christians know "love your neighbor as yourself" by heart, but when they meet a real person, they don't know where to begin loving. Loving the coworker who always opposes you, loving the child who worries you, loving the family member whose words hurt you: these two sentences test us every single day.
Our lives are often too complicated: our calendars are packed, the group chat messages never end, and decisions big and small leave us breathless.

Maybe we need to return to the summary. Just as scientists condensed twenty equations into four, we can take many of life's tangles back to two simple questions: Is this loving God? Is this loving people?

Let me give an example. It's Sunday morning, you're tired, and you're wrestling with whether to come to church. You can list a hundred reasons: you went to bed too late last night, the weather's bad, last week's sermon was a bit long… But if you return to the summary and ask, "Is this loving God?", the answer becomes much clearer.

Here's another example. A family member says something that upsets you, and you really want to snap back and win the argument. In that moment ask, "Is this loving people?" You may find that winning the argument but losing the relationship isn't worth it.

Friends, the summary doesn't make life rigid; it makes life free. Just as physicists with a few simple laws can freely design all kinds of machines, we who have the summary of loving God and loving people can freely make the right choices in endlessly changing situations.
Now let's bring this simplicity into our lives. I'll share three 321 principles.

First, the Bible is my standard. When facing a complicated decision, ask two questions first: Is this loving God? Is this loving people? Many things that look complicated become clear when measured with these two rulers.

Second, the order of relationships: God, self, others, tasks. Put the most important thing first, and life is no longer chaotic. Often we feel things are a mess not because there's too much to do, but because the order is upside down: tasks come before people, and people come before God. Set the order right, like tidying up an equation, and everything becomes clear.

Here's a simple way to check: open your calendar for this week and see where God is. Where is your family? Where are the people around you who need you? If only tasks are left on your calendar, it may be time to reorder things.

Third, practice. Truth is not in memorizing but in living it out. In the eight steps of changing our mindset, "conviction" must always be followed by "practice." When you understand today that "loving God and loving people is the summary," nod and say "Amen," that's conviction. But going home and showing your family a little more patience, giving a coworker one more word of encouragement, that's practice.

And practice doesn't have to be big. A phone call to check in, a willingness to apologize first, a stretch of time with your phone put away, really listening to someone: each is a line of the summary written into your life.

Primes, the Atoms of Numbers: The Wisdom of Counting Our Days
So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom. (Psalm 90:12)

Brothers and sisters, today we're going to meet a group of numbers with a lot of personality. They have one distinctive trait: they're "loners." Apart from 1 and themselves, nothing can divide them evenly.
2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13… These numbers that can only be divided evenly by 1 and themselves are called primes.

You might say, "Pastor, isn't this just middle school math? What's there to talk about?" Don't underestimate them! When you shop online or transfer money on your phone today, what protects you behind the scenes may very well be these ordinary-looking primes. The simplest numbers guard the most important secrets.
Every Number Has a Unique Recipe

Why do primes matter? Because every whole number greater than 1 can be broken down into a product of primes in exactly one way. Take 12, for example: it's 2 times 2 times 3. However you break it down, when you get to the bottom it's always these three primes, no more and no less.

It's like atoms in chemistry. Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, and everything can be broken down into atoms. Numbers are the same: every whole number can be broken down into primes. That's why we say primes are the atoms of numbers.
A Prime Too Big to Write Out
So how big can a prime get? In October 2024, the largest prime known at the time was found: 2 to the power of 136,279,841, minus 1. If you wrote this number out, it would have 41,024,320 digits.
Just imagine printing it as a book. It would probably take several thick volumes, and not a single digit could be misprinted. People go to enormous effort to find a single prime.
But the Bible tells us that God is even more careful than this when it comes to counting.
But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. (Matthew 10:30)
We need lots of computers to find one large prime, but God knows even how many hairs are on your head. He is not a God of rough estimates; he is precise, attentive and faithful.
2. Infinitely Many Primes: A Proof Unchanged for Two Thousand Years
Will we ever run out of primes? The larger the numbers, the sparser the primes. Could they stop altogether at some point?
More than 2,300 years ago, Euclid gave a beautiful proof in Book IX of his Elements. Let me tell it as a little story, and I'm sure you'll follow it.

Suppose someone says, "There are only finitely many primes, and I have the complete list right here." All right, let's multiply every prime on that list together and then add 1, giving us a new number.
Divide this new number by any prime on the list, and there's always a remainder of 1; it never divides evenly. So none of this new number's prime factors can be on the list.
That means the list must have missed some primes! No matter how long a list you bring me, I can use this method to find one that slipped through the net. So there are infinitely many primes.

There's one little detail to notice here: the new number itself isn't necessarily prime. For example, 2 times 3 times 5 times 7 times 11 times 13, plus 1, equals 30031. That isn't prime; it equals 59 times 509. But neither 59 nor 509 is on the original list, so the proof still holds.
Friends, this proof held more than two thousand years ago, it still holds today, and it will still hold a thousand years from now. The patterns of the primes never change.

That leads us to a reasonable thought: this reflects an order of truth established by a faithful God. People change, dynasties change, technology changes, but the truth God placed in numbers doesn't change one bit.

Think about it: over two thousand years, how many empires have risen and fallen, how many theories have come into fashion and been discarded. What people wore, what they ate, which idols they worshiped back then are now museum exhibits. But the proof Euclid wrote down can be picked up by any high school student today and checked step by step, without changing a single word.
Truth like that gives us peace. Our faith is built on a foundation that unchanging too: God's Word lasts even longer than the proof about the primes.
Easy to Mix, Hard to Separate

Primes have another special property. Let's use paint as an example: pouring two paints together and stirring them is easy, but separating the mixed color back into the original two paints is extremely hard.

Multiplying two large primes is like mixing paint; a computer does it in an instant. But if you're given only the product and asked to split it back into the original two primes, it's extremely difficult.

RSA encryption, published in 1978, relies on exactly this property. Much of the security of today's online shopping and bank transfers is built on primes. Every time you pay on your phone, you're under the protection of prime numbers.

Of course, scientists also honestly point out that, in theory, a sufficiently powerful quantum computer could use a method called Shor's algorithm to factor numbers quickly and break RSA. Whether and when such a quantum computer can be built is still in development, so cryptographers are developing new encryption methods.

Up close, primes look chaotic: sometimes two apart, sometimes far apart, as though they were playing hide-and-seek with mathematicians. But overall they follow a pattern: the larger the numbers, the sparser the primes, in a roughly predictable way.

In 1859, Riemann proposed a conjecture about the primes that remains unsolved to this day. Mathematicians have pursued the secrets of the primes for more than two thousand years, and many remain unsolved.
It is the glory of God to conceal a thing, but the glory of kings is to search out a matter. (Proverbs 25:2)

God delights to conceal things so that people will search them out. He's like a father who loves his children and hides presents in corners of the house so the kids can search for them excitedly. When they find them, the children are happy, and so is the father.

If the father simply pushed the presents into his children's hands, of course they'd still be happy, but they'd miss the fun of searching, and miss a time of playing with their father. God hides some secrets not to make things hard for us, but to invite us to seek him and know him all our lives.

Reading the Bible is like that too. Some passages you understand the moment you read them, like picking up a candy left on the table. Others you have to read many times, pray over and meditate on, and even live through certain experiences, before you suddenly understand. The joy of that moment is something no one else can find for you.
Here's another interesting phenomenon. North America has periodical cicadas that emerge en masse only every 13 or 17 years, and both 13 and 17 are primes.

Why is that? Scientists have proposed several hypotheses. One holds that prime-numbered cycles rarely "collide" with predators that have shorter cycles, and computer models suggest such cycles could be favored by natural selection. Another holds that prime cycles mean broods with different cycles seldom emerge in the same year, reducing hybridization.

But I need to say honestly that these are only hypotheses still under study and should not be presented as settled. We can enjoy this wonderful phenomenon without claiming certainty about what is still uncertain.

This is a very important attitude for Christians: toward God we have firm faith; toward scientific details still under study, we stay humble and patient. We don't need to rush to a conclusion about every phenomenon, because truth isn't afraid of time, and truth isn't afraid of being checked.
How do primes come into our lives? I'd like to share three 321 principles.

First, the Holy Spirit is my guide. When God has hidden something, we ask the Holy Spirit to open it; where we don't yet understand, we keep seeking. Mathematicians haven't given up on the Riemann hypothesis, and we shouldn't give up easily on God's Word either. If you can't understand a passage today, ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light, read it again tomorrow, and one day it will suddenly become clear.

Second, from the temporary to the eternal. Counting our days means arranging our time with eternity in view. Moses asked God to "teach us to count our days," because our days are limited and each one is precious. Rather than letting time quietly slip away while scrolling on our phones, let's ask: what one thing today has eternal value?

Third, 235, spiritual companions. Just as two large primes multiplied together make a strong lock that others find hard to open, two spiritual companions watching over each other can be a strong protection. The enemy has a hard time breaking through a pair of companions who pray for and remind one another. Find a spiritual companion, and walk the road of faith together.
This week's action: work out roughly how many days you have lived, that is, your age times 365, and write it in your notebook. Then write down one thing you will do for God today.
Brothers and sisters, think about it: how many days have you lived? Ten thousand? Twenty thousand? Every one of those days is a gift God has counted and given.

God has numbered even the hairs on our heads, and he counts every one of our days. He is a precise, attentive and faithful God. The primes have not changed in two thousand years, and his love will never change.
Let's quietly reflect: If my days are counted by God, how will I use today?

Faithful Father, you have numbered the hairs on my head and you count my days. Give me a heart of wisdom so that I do not waste a single day you give me, but spend it on what has eternal value. And please give me a spiritual companion, so that we can watch over each other and walk in your ways together. In Jesus' name, Amen.

Zoom In and Zoom In Again: Fractals and a Life Transformed from Glory to Glory
But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit. (2 Corinthians 3:18)
Brothers and sisters, let me start with a quiz question. It's very simple: how long is the coastline of Britain?
You might say, "Pastor, you can look that up online in a second." But the answer is surprising: it depends on the length of your ruler.

If you use a ruler 100 kilometers long and measure section by section, you'll skip over many bays, and you'll get a shorter length. Switch to a 1-kilometer ruler, and you can take in more of the twists and turns, so the length grows. Switch to a 1-meter ruler, and you count even the bumps of the rocks, so the length grows longer still.
The shorter the ruler, the longer the coastline! That sounds absurd, doesn't it?

In 1967, the mathematician Benoit Mandelbrot published an article in the journal Science titled "How Long Is the Coast of Britain?" With this seemingly simple question, he opened up a whole new kind of geometry. Today, let's look at this geometry together, and at God's work in our lives.
How precious to me are your thoughts, God! How vast is their sum! If I would count them, they are more in number than the sand. When I wake up, I am still with you. (Psalm 139:17–18)
1. What Is a Fractal? The Part Looks Like the Whole
Mandelbrot later gave these shapes a name: "fractals." The defining feature of a fractal is "self-similarity," which means that if you zoom in on a small part of it, it looks much like the whole.

It's a bit like Russian nesting dolls: open one, and there's another identical one inside; open that, and there's another. Only fractals are even more amazing, because every corner of them hides dolls like this.

Take coastlines first. Mandelbrot estimated the fractal dimension of Britain's west coast at about 1.25. What does that mean? A line is one-dimensional, a plane is two-dimensional, and a winding coastline falls somewhere between a line and a plane, so it's 1.25-dimensional. It's more "crowded" than a line, yet it doesn't fill a whole patch of the plane.

Next, ferns. A fern frond is made of many smaller leaflets, and each leaflet looks like a miniature fern frond. The mathematician Michael Barnsley could draw a very lifelike fern on a computer using just four simple transformation rules.

Then there's Romanesco cauliflower. The next time you see one at the market, look closely: every little spire is made of even smaller spires arranged in spirals. It's practically a math lesson growing in the vegetable garden.

What is a fractal like? It's like a great tree. The trunk splits into large branches, the large branches into smaller ones, and the smaller ones into twigs. The same branching pattern repeats at every size. So whether you look at a tree from a distance or step close to look at one branch, you see the same pattern.
The most famous example of a fractal is the Mandelbrot set. Where does it come from? Just one rule: z becomes z squared plus c, and you calculate it over and over, again and again.

That one simple rule produces an infinitely complex shape. Zoom in ten times, and new patterns appear; zoom in a hundred times, and more new patterns appear; however far you zoom in, you can never see it all.

In 1998, the Japanese mathematician Mitsuhiro Shishikura proved something astonishing: although the boundary of the Mandelbrot set is a "line," its Hausdorff dimension equals 2. In other words, this line is so crumpled that it almost fills the entire plane.

But we also need to be clear: fractals in nature are self-similar only within a certain range and stop at some level of magnification. A tree stops branching once it reaches its finest twigs; only mathematical fractals can be zoomed in on forever.

A 2021 study found that the cauliflower's fractal form comes from changes in the gene network that controls flowering: places that were meant to become flowers repeatedly grow new branching points instead. This is a very recent finding, and the details are still being explored.
One simple rule produces endless beauty at every scale. That leads us to a reasonable thought: it reflects the Creator's abundant wisdom and goodness.
The psalmist says God's thoughts outnumber the sand. Fractals are like a small window God opens before our eyes, letting us glimpse his infinitely rich thoughts.

Here's something interesting. When a person paints a picture and you zoom in, all you see are brushstrokes and grains of pigment; the closer you look, the rougher it gets. But the world God made often gets more fascinating the closer you look: a leaf, a cauliflower, a stretch of coastline, magnified, becomes a whole new world. Human work can't stand up to close inspection, but God's work grows more beautiful the more closely you look.
And the psalmist says that the thoughts of this God, whose thoughts are infinitely rich, are "to me." He doesn't only pour his care into cauliflowers; he pours his care into you and me.
3. The Same Pattern in Great and Small
Fractals teach us something very important: the same pattern holds in large things and in small things.
Jesus actually taught this "fractal principle" long ago.
He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. (Luke 16:10)

Who a person is in little things is who they are in big things. Someone who is impatient with a restaurant server will find it hard to be gentle at home; someone who is careless with small accounts will find it hard to be reliable in big matters. On the other hand, someone who is willing to wash the dishes properly, answer messages clearly and show up on time has a character that, like a fractal, looks the same at any magnification.
The Image of Christ Reproduced at Every Level

God's work in us is like this too. He doesn't change just one corner of our lives; he wants the same image of Christ to be reproduced again and again at every level of our lives: at church, at home, at work, in our thoughts and intentions, even in a glance or a single word.
But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit. (2 Corinthians 3:18)
"From glory to glory": just like zooming in on a fractal, at every level we discover new beauty. It's an ongoing process, not something finished in a day.
Maybe you feel discouraged: "I've been a believer for so many years. Why am I still the same?" Please don't lose heart; God is still at work.

Think about that great tree. When the seed first sprouts, it's just one tiny stem, and you can't tell what it will grow into. But its branching pattern was written inside it from the start. Year after year, following the same pattern, it grows layer upon layer of branches, until at last it becomes a great tree where the birds can nest.

The pattern of Christ in your life is like that. Today it may be just a tiny stem, but as long as you keep beholding the Lord's glory and keep drawing near to him, that pattern will grow out layer by layer. Not by your own striving, but "even as from the Lord, the Spirit."
being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ. (Philippians 1:6)
Stepping from fractals into daily life, I'd like to share three 321 principles.

First, selflessness, the self-emptied life. Paul said, "it is no longer I that live, but Christ living in me." Selflessness doesn't mean destroying yourself; it means letting the pattern of Christ be reproduced at every level of my life, from the great direction of my life down to the tone of a single sentence.

Second, 920, the fruit of the Spirit. The fruit of the Spirit often grows from the smallest things. One act of patience, one gentle word, one decision to forgive: these are the fractals of character. The fruit you bear in small things today, magnified, is what your whole life will look like.

Third, multiplication. Spiritual life reproduces like a fractal: I follow Christ, then lead others to follow Christ, and they in turn lead someone else. The same pattern is reproduced generation after generation. This is exactly how we build God's kingdom system: not by one person doing something huge, but by each person passing on the pattern of Christ.
This week's action: choose one of the smallest everyday tasks, such as being on time, clearing the dishes or replying to messages, and do it faithfully and well as an offering to the Lord.

Brothers and sisters, today is also the last stop in our Mathematics Hall. All along the way, from why math works, Fibonacci spirals, the beauty of symmetry, the most beautiful equation, infinity and simple laws to primes and today's fractals, we have seen one thing: the universe is written in God's language.
May every calculation and every moment of wonder become worship, and may you share the glory you have seen with the people around you.

When you get home, find a leaf, a twig or a head of cauliflower, and look closely at how it branches. Look from the large to the small, then from the small back to the large. Then quietly reflect: In the smallest things of my life (a word, a glance, a habit), do I also reflect the pattern of Christ?

Lord Jesus, reproduce your pattern at every level of my life: at home, at work, and in my thoughts and intentions. Make me faithful in the smallest things, and transform me from glory to glory, to be more like you. Use me to pass your pattern on to the people around me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
