Probability: The Mother and the One in Seventy-Three Million
The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from Yahweh. (Proverbs 16:33)
Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! There is a number that once sent a mother to prison. The number is: one in seventy-three million.

In 1999, in England, a solicitor named Sally Clark stood in the dock. Her first son died suddenly in 1996, and her second son died in early 1998, at only eight weeks old. She was charged with murder. In court a very famous pediatrician testified that the chance of two cot deaths in a row in a family like this was one in seventy-three million.

Think about it: if you were a juror and heard that number, what would you think? One in seventy-three million, harder than winning the lottery, so she must have done it? She was convicted, and sentenced to life in prison.

But that number was wrong, and wrong by a wide margin. The Royal Statistical Society later issued a public statement expressing its concern about the case. In 2003 she finally won her appeal and was set free. The direct reason was that the prosecution pathologist had not disclosed a key microbiological report. But by then this mother, who had already lost two children, had lost several more years, and had carried the name of “baby killer” for several years. In 2007 she left this world, only in her forties.

Today we walk into the Mathematics Hall to talk about probability. Why begin with such a heavy story? Because we Christians also love to quote numbers. We often hear it said: “The odds of the universe forming like this are lower than a tornado blowing through a junkyard and assembling a Boeing 747, so there must be a God!” Brothers and sisters, that sentence sounds satisfying. But if our way of calculating probability is the same kind as that doctor’s, then we may be going into battle with a blunt knife. Today I want to take you through sharpening it.
The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from Yahweh. (Proverbs 16:33)
1. A Winning Receipt Won’t Make Anyone Call the Police
A low probability by itself proves nothing
Let’s first see where that number went wrong.

The first mistake: the doctor took the probability of one cot death, one in eight thousand five hundred and forty-three, and multiplied it by itself. That is the same as assuming the deaths of the first child and the second child have nothing to do with each other, like tossing a coin twice. But the same family has the same genes and the same environment. That assumption had no basis.

The second mistake goes deeper, and it has a name: the “prosecutor’s fallacy.” This mistake mixes up two sentences that sound alike. The first: “If she is innocent, the chance of this happening is very low.” The second: “The chance that she is innocent is very low.”

These two are far apart. Let me give an example: the chance of any one person becoming the head of a country is extremely low. But you cannot turn it around and say: the person sitting in that seat today is probably not human, is he?

Back to Clark’s case. Two cot deaths are rare, but a mother killing her own two babies one after the other is also extremely rare! What a court really has to compare is which of these two rare explanations is relatively more likely. To show the number on only one side is not doing mathematics. It is frightening people.
Why nobody calls the police over a receipt

Let’s use something every Taiwanese friend knows: the Uniform Invoice, the government receipt lottery. To win the special prize of ten million dollars you must match all eight digits, and the chance is one in a hundred million. One in a hundred million! But the draw happens every two months, a winner always turns up, and people often win. Does anyone call the police because of that? No.

But what if the same person won the special prize three draws in a row? I guarantee you, the people from the tax bureau would come to “have tea” with him, which is how we say they would call him in for questioning.

That is strange. Winning three times in a row is hard, but those three numbers have exactly the same chance as any other three numbers! Why is our reaction different? Because for the latter, there is another explanation waiting beside it: “Someone tampered with it.” That explanation can make the result not surprising at all.

Brothers and sisters, this is the most important sentence today: a low probability by itself proves nothing. For it to become evidence, there must be another explanation that would have predicted it better.

The earliest person to say this was interesting, because he was a pastor. The Reverend Bayes was an English Presbyterian minister who died in 1761. His friend Price put in order the papers he left behind and submitted them to the Royal Society two years later. Today, whether it is a spam filter or a medical reading, the descendants of his line of thought are still at work. The notes that a minister left behind outside of his preaching are at work in your phone every day.
Spiritual meaning: do not bear witness with false weights

So I exhort you, brothers and sisters: God does not need us to cook the books for Him. Proverbs says, “A false balance is an abomination to Yahweh,” and that applies to statistics just the same. If a friend asks you about your faith, you can tell him what you believe, and you can also tell him what you do not know. Do not casually toss out a startling number you saw online, with no idea what its denominator is. Once that number is exposed, what gets doubted along with it is the gospel you preach.
2. Our Intuition Is Very Bad at Math
Birthdays in a room, and that positive result

Let’s play another little game. How many people must be in a room for there to be an even chance that two of them share a birthday? Many people guess a hundred or more, because a year has three hundred and sixty-five days. The answer is twenty-three. With seventy people, the chance is already ninety-nine point nine percent.

Why? Because you are thinking “someone else shares my day,” but what has to be compared is every pair of people. Twenty-three people make two hundred and fifty-three pairs. So the next time you find two brothers in your small group with the same birthday, everyone can celebrate happily, but there is no need to say right away that it is a special arrangement from God.

Here is one that matters more. A certain disease strikes one person in every thousand. The test is ninety-nine percent accurate. Today you get your report: positive. What is the chance that you really have the disease? Ninety-nine percent?

Let me work it out for you. Among a thousand people, about one is really sick, and the test will probably catch him. There are nine hundred and ninety-nine healthy people, and one percent of them will be wrongly flagged, about ten. So among eleven positive reports, only one is really a sick person, about nine percent. Of course, this is a simplified classroom calculation; when you get a report you should still see a doctor and listen to what the doctor says. But you see, with the same report, the person who knows how to calculate and the person who does not will sleep very differently that night!
Coincidences are more common than we think

Two statisticians, Diaconis and Mosteller, made a special study of coincidences. They stated a very practical principle: given a large enough sample, even the most bizarre things can happen. There are more than eight billion people in the world, and how many things does each one go through every day? So every day someone meets a one-in-ten-million coincidence. And who will bear witness to the things that did not happen?
Spiritual meaning: true witness, clear discernment

This is not telling us not to believe in God’s guidance. Many brothers and sisters have prayed and then met with incredible arrangements, and their gratitude is real. But the Bible asks us to test things. We do not use coincidences to decide whether to resign, whether to marry, or whether to donate a house. Ask for the Lord’s word as the standard, and look together with spiritual companions, because when a person wants something too badly, confirmations are all over the street.

Good, now let’s take the sharpened knife and use it on the big question. Some physical constants, if they were only slightly different, would mean no stars, no chemistry and perhaps no life. This is called fine-tuning. The Cosmos Hall has already covered this topic. Today we ask only one thing: how much can probability help here?

An Australian astrophysicist, Luke Barnes, wrote a long review paper in 2012 that organizes the literature in this area, and he also criticized many of the claims of Victor Stenger, who argued that fine-tuning can all be explained away. But notice that Barnes specifically says in his abstract that he is not defending any conclusion based on fine-tuning. You see, that is how a good scholar is: facts are facts, conclusions are conclusions.

According to what we just learned, for a probability to carry evidential weight we must ask: is there another explanation that would have predicted this result better? The theist says: if there is a Creator who wants life to exist, a universe that permits life is not surprising. That is a reasonable consideration.

But there are serious responses from the other side. Some say: perhaps there are a great many universes, one of them is bound to win, and of course we would only appear in the winning one. That is the multiverse. It has its troubles too: at present there is no direct observation, and some philosophers also hold that what turns up at another table cannot explain our table. Another response says: we have seen only one universe, a sample size of one, so how can we talk about probability? Perhaps there are deeper laws of physics.

I also have to tell you honestly that our side has problems too. First, the denominator problem. If a constant could in principle be any number, then the range is infinite, and probability cannot be spread evenly over it, so it is hard to say which value is “improbable.” The McGrews and Vestrup pointed this out in 2001 in the philosophy journal Mind. Brothers and sisters, when we cannot even say clearly what the denominator is, we should be especially careful with numbers like “one in ten to the power of several hundred.”

Second, Hoyle’s Boeing 747. That analogy was originally about the origin of life, and his own conclusion was not the God of the Bible; he argued that life came from space. People who study the origin of life also do not claim a one-step assembly. How life began has not been solved to this day, and that is a fact we can state honestly; but please stop using this airplane.

Third, even if the probability argument holds, the most it can reach is a Creator with a purpose. It cannot calculate His name, and it cannot calculate whether He loves you. That brings us to our third point.
Spiritual meaning: the heaviest casting of lots in the world

The Bible is actually not naive about probability at all. Ecclesiastes says the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, but time and chance happen to them all. The Bible admits that under the sun, the course of the world is just this hard to predict. When Ruth went to glean, the text says she “happened to come” to the field of Boaz. But that happening brought her into David’s family line.

Then they said to one another, “Let’s not tear it, but cast lots for it to decide whose it will be,” that the Scripture might be fulfilled, which says, “They parted my garments among them. They cast lots for my clothing.” Therefore the soldiers did these things. (John 19:24)

Brothers and sisters, picture that scene. On the cross, a man is dying. Beneath the cross, a few soldiers are gambling for a garment, and they may even be laughing. To them it was only an afternoon’s luck. But John says this fulfilled the Scripture.

This is not saying that every cruel thing in the world is God’s good pleasure. I want to say this especially to friends who have lost a child or someone they love: no one has the right to stand in front of you and explain your tears with the words “this is all God’s arrangement.” Sally Clark’s grief cannot be told in the space of one sermon illustration. What the cross tells us is that God did not stand outside suffering calculating odds. He came in Himself.
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. (Romans 5:8)

Today we learned one simple thing: a low probability is not in itself evidence. We do not need to exaggerate numbers to protect God, and He does not need us to cook the books for Him. The Bible is my standard, so I use it to discern coincidences, and I do not use coincidences to rewrite it. People matter more than tasks, so I see the person behind the number. Let God be God, so I do not have to be able to calculate everything.

There is a small assignment for this week. The next time you receive a startling statistic in a group chat, or a testimony that is amazingly coincidental, first ask two questions: what is the denominator? What other explanations are there? When you have asked, decide whether to forward it. If a friend is willing to talk, you can gently ask: “Have you ever had something happen that was so coincidental you could hardly believe it? How did you see it afterward?” And then listen well.
Let us be quiet for a moment, and think of something in your life that was “too coincidental,” and also of something you still do not understand today. Place both before the Lord.

Let us pray together: Lord who rules over all, there is so much under the sun that I cannot calculate. Thank You that on the cross You have already shown Your love. Keep me from both superstition about coincidence and disregard for Your guidance; and when I do not understand, let me rest in handing tomorrow into Your hands. In Jesus’ name, amen.

2. Have you ever taken a coincidence as God’s guidance? How do you see it afterward? How can we avoid both superstition and disregard for God’s guidance?
3. When a friend meets with misfortune, we often rush to explain. How does the scene beneath the cross change the way you walk with those who suffer?
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. (John 1:1)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Imagine a typhoon night. The wind and rain are fierce, and the TV says the district where your mother lives is flooded. You call, but can’t get through. You keep looking at your phone, again and again. At last, ding, your mother sends two words: “Safe.”
In that instant your whole body loosens. Tears may even come. If the same two words arrived on the neighbor’s phone next door, he would glance at them and go on eating his instant noodles.

So tell me, what is actually inside those two words? If you took the phone apart, you could find a little electric charge and a few tiny lit points, but you could not find that sigh of relief or that tear.

Today we are walking into a very young exhibit hall in the Mathematics Hall, one that has changed the whole world: information. Let me begin with an interesting piece of news. In 2017 two scientists in New York stored six files in synthetic DNA, the man-made version of the molecule in our cells. What were the six files? A complete computer operating system, a French film from 1895, a fifty-dollar Amazon gift card, a computer virus, the plaque design carried by the Pioneer space probes, and a paper from 1948.

Brothers and sisters, that list is funny, like things a person grabs at random when moving house. Later they read the data back, without a single error. The film was still that film, and the paper was still that paper. The paper changed, the ink changed, even the kind of material changed, and something stayed. What was that something?
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. (John 1:1-2)
1. The Information in a Coin Toss

The paper that was stored in DNA was written by Claude Shannon, an engineer at Bell Labs, and its title was “A Mathematical Theory of Communication.” Before him, “information” was only an everyday word; after him, it became something that can be calculated. Your phone in your hand, the Wi-Fi at home, streaming movies, all owe thanks to him.

He did something very bold. Right at the start he declared that the meaning of a message has nothing to do with the engineering problem. Listen to that: a man who studied communication said that meaning does not matter!

So what did he count? He asked only one thing: how many possibilities does this message rule out for you? Toss a fair coin, heads and tails half and half, and when the result comes out you get one bit of information. The word bit was suggested by his colleague Tukey, and Shannon honestly noted this in the paper. What if the coin has heads on both sides? The toss holds no suspense, and the information is zero.
So the more surprising, the more information. That the sun rises in the east every morning is not news; if one day it came up in the west, it would be the headline all over the world.
How many bits are mother’s two words worth?

Let’s go back to those two words, “Safe.” By Shannon’s formula, your phone and the neighbor’s phone receive the same amount of data. The formula doesn’t care who the mother is. That is not a flaw in the formula; that is exactly what makes it powerful. Precisely because it doesn’t care about meaning, the same line can carry love letters and also carry bills.
But people live precisely for the part the formula does not count. We spend a lot of money on data, and what we really want is for someone to speak to us.
Spiritual meaning: you are the one being spoken to

The God of the Bible is, from the beginning, a God who speaks. God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. That tells us something very comforting: behind this world there may not be a silent probability, but One who speaks. This is a confession of faith, not something the formula calculates. But, brothers and sisters, when you can’t sleep at midnight and open your Bible, you can believe you are not just processing data. A Lord who knows you is speaking to you.
2. No Mass, Yet Inseparable from Matter
In the same year as Shannon, 1948, the mathematician Wiener wrote a book called Cybernetics. In it he left a famous line: information is information, not matter or energy.

That makes good sense. Take the Bible in your hand and say I burn it; you go to the bookstore and buy a new one, and not one word of the content is missing. The psalms you have memorized don’t even need the book. That is why, even when your hard drive is full, it doesn’t get noticeably heavier. The content itself seems to take up no weight.

But another physicist, Landauer, did not quite agree with describing information as so ethereal. In 1991 he wrote an article whose title was “Information Is Physical.” He said, have you ever seen information that is not written on anything? It always has to be carved in stone, printed on paper, stored in a circuit, or remembered in your nerve cells.

As early as 1961 he worked out that erasing one bit must cost a little heat. How much? At room temperature about three times ten to the minus twenty-one joules, so small it is hardly human language. But in 2012 a team really did the experiment: they held a glass microparticle with optical tweezers and let it move between two positions, one counting as zero and one as one, then erased that bit, and saw the heat come right up against this lower limit.

Even deleting one character costs something! Brothers and sisters, you don’t need to feel guilty about deleting messages, since you can’t feel that bit of heat at all. But when some words have left your mouth, taking them back costs a great deal, and we have all been through that.
At this point many Christian friends get excited: “DNA is information, information must come from a mind, so there must be a God!” This argument has to be taken apart carefully.

The part that is fact is this: cells really do use sixty-four triplet codons to map to twenty amino acids and stop signals. DNA’s capacity is also truly astonishing; the 2017 team estimated that in theory one gram could hold two hundred and fifteen petabytes. But what they actually stored was only about two megabytes, and the synthesis alone cost seven thousand dollars, so it is still a long way from everyday use.

The part that is inference is where the dispute begins. In his 2009 book Signature in the Cell, Meyer argues: the source we actually know to produce large amounts of functional information is intelligence, and since there is no accepted chemical pathway for the origin of life, intelligence is the best explanation. This argument is worth reading seriously.

But the other side has serious responses too. Many biologists say that random variation plus natural selection can accumulate functional information in a genome, and Schneider ran a computer simulation in 2000 to demonstrate it. Some critics also think this kind of argument really packages “we don’t currently know” as an answer. Even the Christian biologist Falk has publicly criticized the book. The philosopher Griffiths goes further: he thinks the very statement “genes carry information” is often a misleading metaphor.

So today I will not tell you that “information theory proves God.” I will tell you: it is a philosophical question worth discussing, Christians stand at different positions on it, and we can respect one another.
Spiritual meaning: the word has to have a body

But Landauer’s line, “information must be written on something,” makes me think of something beautiful. Human love is like this too. It cannot exist only in the head. It has to be written into a meal, into company at a hospital, into the drive to pick you up in the middle of the night.
Now let’s look at John’s Gospel. Some will say: “In the beginning was the Word. Isn’t this Word just information? The bottom layer of the universe is information; don’t physicists say so too?”

The physicist Wheeler did offer a fascinating idea called it from bit: every physical thing may ultimately derive from answers to yes-or-no questions. But Wheeler plainly called it a working hypothesis, a direction to guide research, not yet a conclusion.

More important, John’s Word and Shannon’s information are simply not the same thing. Shannon’s information deliberately ignores meaning; John’s Word is full of meaning, full of grace, full of truth, and is a Person who was with God and who is God. To draw an equals sign between the two both misunderstands Shannon and shrinks John.
The Word became flesh and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth. (John 1:14)

Brothers and sisters, this verse is astonishing. Remember our question? The same content can change carriers. God’s word came through a pillar of fire, through the book of the law, through the mouths of the prophets. When the time had fully come, the Word took on the most fragile carrier of all: a crying baby in the manger of Bethlehem, a body that grows tired, grows hungry and bleeds.

When a person loves you, he can write you a letter, or he can walk over himself. Our God did both. At Golgotha He let that carrier be torn apart, and the world thought that this blow had erased the message for good. By Landauer’s account, erasing has a cost. The cost on the cross was paid by Him. But on the third day the Word walked out of the tomb, and the message was not erased; it has come all the way to us today.
The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever. (Isaiah 40:8)
Spiritual meaning: let the Word become flesh in you

So the first foundation of 321 is: Jesus is my example. How did He love people? He came Himself. Our generation has everything, and a message can reach the other side of the earth in a second, yet there are so many lonely people. However many stickers you send, none compares with a person walking to your side and sitting down.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. Your child will remember the principles you taught, but will remember even more the day you put down your phone and crouched down to look at him. The word has to have a body, and the gospel has to have a body too, and that is you and me.

Let’s return to that typhoon night. What let you breathe out was those two words, or the person who typed them? Brothers and sisters, Shannon can work out the bits for us, Landauer can work out the heat, and scientists can store a paper in DNA. All of this is remarkable and worth thanking God for. But the deepest longing of our lives is to have One who knows me speak to me. The good news of the gospel is that the Word has come in person to live among us.

This week’s action: pick someone you usually only text, and phone them or visit them in person. If you have a friend who does not yet believe, you can ask: “Has anyone said something to you lately that moved you deeply? Why do the same words make such a different impression coming from different people?” Listen until he is finished, and then tell him about the words a Lord has spoken to you.

Please open your phone, find a message that once comforted you, and look at it. Think: was it those bits that comforted you, or the person who sent the message? And ask yourself too: when I read the Bible, am I processing data, or listening to the Lord speak?

Let us pray together: Living Word, Lord Jesus, thank You that You did not simply send me a letter but came among us Yourself. Make Your words come alive in me, and let every word I speak carry grace and truth. In Jesus’ name, amen.

2. How would you now explain the argument “DNA is information, so there must be a designer” to a friend, in a way that is both confident and honest?
3. Which loving word do you want to turn into an action with a body this week? Who is it for? Share it next time.
Chaos: The Next Month You Cannot Calculate
“For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,” says Yahweh. (Isaiah 55:8)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Let me ask you a question. The weather app on your phone can tell you it will rain at three tomorrow afternoon. So why is there no app that dares to tell you whether it will rain on the fifth of next month?

You might say: the computers aren’t big enough, there isn’t enough data, just wait a few more years. That is reasonable, but it is only half of the answer. The other half was discovered in 1961 by a meteorologist who was having a cup of coffee.

His name was Lorenz, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and he was using a computer that looks clunky to us today to run a simplified weather model. One day he wanted to look again at a stretch of results. To save time, he did not rerun it from the beginning. He copied a number from the middle of the printout and typed it back in: zero point five zero six. But what the computer had actually stored was zero point five zero six one two seven. He had left off three decimal places. How big a difference is that? Less than three ten-thousandths. Then he went off for his coffee.

When he came back, he was startled. The new weather started out almost exactly like the old, but the further it went, the less alike they were, until in the end it was a completely different weather. His first thought was that the computer was broken. It wasn’t. And there was no random number anywhere in the equations. No dice. Every step followed the rules. Friends, what he had run into was the ceiling of human weather forecasting.
Who can count the clouds by wisdom? (Job 38:37)
God once asked Job this question. For more than two thousand years people took it as poetry. After Lorenz, it sounds like a math problem.
1. Two sesame seeds in the scallion pancake

Our topic today is chaos. In everyday speech, chaos means a big mess; a child’s bedroom is chaos. But in mathematics it has a precise meaning: the rules are completely fixed, yet the outcome is extremely sensitive to the starting conditions, and therefore cannot be predicted in the long run.

In 1963 Lorenz published a paper that boiled this down to three very short equations. A middle-school student would not be frightened by them. But the path those three equations trace never repeats and never leaves a certain region, and when it is drawn it looks like a pair of wings.

How can that be? Let me invite you into the kitchen. Suppose you are kneading scallion-pancake dough, the kind we love in Taiwan, and you put two sesame seeds on it, right next to each other. Stretch it, fold it back, stretch it again, fold it back again. After a few rounds, those two seeds that started out touching are far apart, and it is very hard to guess where they are. And yet not one seed has fallen out of the dough.

Stretching makes a tiny miss into a huge miss; folding keeps everything within bounds. That is the secret of chaos. It is unpredictable, but it is not lawless. Weather is the same. You cannot predict one particular day thirty days from now, but you do know that January will not be hotter than July.
Even a middle-school formula can go wild

In 1976 an ecologist named May published an article in the journal Nature. He had originally been studying how animal populations change in size. He pointed out that a formula a middle-school student can work out shows this same behavior, as long as you keep feeding the answer back in.

We have actually tried it: set one parameter to four and start from zero point two; then start again from zero point two plus one ten-millionth. At first the two strings of numbers are almost the same, and by about the twentieth step they have become strangers. A difference of one ten-millionth, used up in twenty steps! May also urged that this kind of simple equation be brought into basic math classes. He was right, because simple rules do not necessarily bring simple results, and we learned that common-sense lesson far too late.
Spiritual meaning: the world is bigger than our spreadsheet

Brothers and sisters, so many of us love spreadsheets. Five-year plans, ten-year plans. Planning is a good thing, and the Bible teaches us to count the cost. But James reminds us that you do not know what your life will be like tomorrow. Chaos adds a footnote to that sentence in the language of mathematics: even if you know every one of the rules, you may still be unable to calculate what lies far ahead.
2. How the butterfly got its wings

You have surely heard of the butterfly effect. Many motivational books say: a butterfly flaps its wings and can set off a hurricane, so your one smile can change the world! A smile is a lovely thing, but that is not what Lorenz said.

Here is what actually happened. In his early years the example Lorenz used was the flapping of a seagull’s wings. In 1972 he was due to speak at the American Association for the Advancement of Science. He had not turned in a title in time, so the session chair, Merilees, made one up for him: “Does the flap of a butterfly’s wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?” Brothers and sisters, did you notice? It is a question. To this day no one has shown that any particular butterfly caused any particular tornado. What it is saying is that tiny differences get amplified layer by layer until a forecast loses its footing.

So should we stop trusting weather forecasts? Quite the opposite. This is humanity’s quietest victory. In 2015 Nature ran a review titled “The quiet revolution of numerical weather prediction.” The authors point out that over the past few decades forecast skill has improved by about one day per decade, so today’s six-day forecast is as good as a five-day forecast was ten years ago. Before a typhoon arrives, you can prepare days ahead, and think how many lives have been saved because of it!

But where is the wall? In 2019 Professor Fuqing Zhang and his colleagues estimated that the limit for midlatitude weather is about two weeks, which is close to what Lorenz himself estimated back then. But science always has a new page to turn. In 2026 two researchers published a study in which they used a machine-learning model to tune the starting conditions in hindsight, and forecast skill could exceed thirty days. They also say honestly that they do not yet know whether such starting conditions can be found in real time, ahead of the event. So where this wall really stands is still being argued over. I will not hand down a verdict today.
Spiritual meaning: do not make the gaps God’s home

Some of you may be excited: “Great! Wherever science can’t calculate, that is where God is at work!” Serious scholars have indeed raised this idea. The physicist and theologian Polkinghorne holds that the unpredictability of chaos may reflect a real openness in the world. But other scholars have replied that the equations of chaos are deterministic, so this is not a true gap.

I want to remind you, do not build God’s house in the gaps. Every time science advances, the gaps get smaller, and does your God not shrink along with them? God’s governance does not depend on what people cannot calculate. In the places where we can calculate, He governs just the same: the sunrise, the tides, the very breath you drew this morning are all in His hand. Today we take chaos only as a lesson in humility, and not as evidence of God stepping in.
“Aren’t two sparrows sold for an assarion coin? Not one of them falls to the ground apart from your Father’s will. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. (Matthew 10:29-30)

When Jesus said this, He knew the market price very well: two sparrows for a coin worth next to nothing. He also knew the weather; He said that when you see a cloud rising in the west, you say it is going to rain. But what He wanted His disciples to see was this: that sentence does not say sparrows never fall. Sparrows do fall, and disciples will suffer. What He said was that the one that falls does not fall outside the Father’s sight.

If you drew Joseph’s life as a line, it would be nothing less than a chaotic curve. A father gives a coat of many colors. The brothers, in a moment’s change of heart, do not kill him but sell him. He is sold into Potiphar’s house. He is falsely accused and thrown into prison. A cupbearer promises to speak up for him, and forgets. If any one of those small turns had been different, history would have been completely different.

He walked that road for many years, and only at the end did he say to his brothers, “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” Brothers and sisters, please notice who is speaking. It is the sufferer himself, saying it many years later. If your friend lost a family member only yesterday, please do not bring this verse to him today. Sitting beside him is worth far more than explaining.
Spiritual meaning: the most unpredictable morning

Let us look at one more line. A disciple betrays his teacher for thirty pieces of silver. A crowd that days earlier shouted Hosanna now shouts for Him to be crucified. A governor washes his hands. Every one of them bears real responsibility, and none of these choices was play-acting. To anyone living through that day, it looked like a tragedy spinning out of control, and everything was lost.

But early on the third day, a few women went to the tomb with spices, and not one of them had predicted what she would see. The most unpredictable morning in all of history was something God had prepared long before.
We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose. (Romans 8:28)

This verse is often used far too lightly. It does not say that everything is good. Cancer is not good, betrayal is not good, a car accident is not good. What Paul is saying is that God is at work in all of it, bringing out His goodness. The ground for that assurance is not something we have calculated. It is the cross and the empty tomb.

Brothers and sisters, there is a passage in Ecclesiastes that I think is the best guide for living in a chaotic world. It says you do not know the way of the wind. So what should we do? Not sit and wait until everything is figured out. The next verse says:
In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening don’t withhold your hand; for you don’t know which will prosper, whether this or that, or whether they both will be equally good. (Ecclesiastes 11:6)

This is what we in 321 mean by letting God be God and people be people. Our place is to be faithful in today’s work; governing tomorrow is God’s place. A great deal of anxiety is really us trying to leave our place and climb into the seat that belongs to God alone. A kind word, a meal, a time of just being with someone: what will it become later? We cannot calculate it. So do it, and entrust the outcome to God. The 920 way of life is exactly this: in every relationship, live out selflessness, and the fruit is borne by the Holy Spirit.

This week’s assignment: do one good deed whose outcome you cannot foresee. Write a thank-you letter, invite a friend to a meal, or pray for someone you have not been in touch with for a long time, and do not track the results. If you get a chance to chat with a friend, you might ask: “Looking back, is there one very small turning point in your life that changed everything that came after?”
Let us be quiet for a moment and think about next month. What is there that you are working hard to control, and simply cannot calculate? Lay it before the Lord.

Let us pray together: Heavenly Father, I cannot even calculate next month’s clouds, much less my own tomorrow. Forgive the pride that wants to sit in Your seat. On the road I cannot see clearly, still let me see the cross and the empty tomb, and let me do today’s work with a peaceful heart. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. Using the scallion-pancake picture, explain how chaos differs from what people usually call “a mess.” What things in your own life have clear rules and yet still cannot be calculated?
2. Looking back over your life, which small turning point changed everything that followed? How did you see it then, and how do you see it now?
3. Romans 8:28 is often used too lightly. If a friend is in the middle of suffering, how would you walk with him? Which words have you decided not to say?
Gödel: Truth Is Bigger Than Proof
For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, even as I was also fully known. (1 Corinthians 13:12)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Today I want to talk about a mathematician whom many people quote and very few have actually read. If you have seen someone on Facebook say, “Gödel proved with mathematics that God exists!” and then seen someone else say, “Gödel proved there is no absolute truth in the world!” then congratulations: both of them are wrong. Today let us get it right together.

Come back with me to September 1930, in Königsberg, Germany. Hilbert, then the most celebrated mathematician in the world, had already retired. He gave a radio address defending pure reason, and ended with ringing words: We must know. We will know. Those words were later carved on his gravestone.
The day before, in the same city, at a small academic conference, a 24-year-old Austrian announced a result. His name was Gödel. From that day on, Hilbert’s dream could never go back to what it was.
For we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when that which is complete has come, then that which is partial will be done away with. (1 Corinthians 13:9-10)

This theorem has conditions, and the conditions must be stated first. A formal system must, first, be consistent: it never proves both a statement and its negation. Second, its axioms can be checked mechanically. Third, it must be strong enough to express basic arithmetic. When those are met, there are two results. The first incompleteness theorem: in this system there must be a statement that can be neither proved nor refuted. The second incompleteness theorem: this system cannot prove its own consistency.

Let me use a comparison for the second theorem. A company cannot rely on its own accounting alone to assure the outside world that its books are clean. The books may be perfectly correct, but the sentence “the books are right” has to come from an outside audit. And the outside auditor has its own books to check. Friends, it is much like telling your child to grade his own homework.

His approach is truly beautiful. He gave every mathematical formula a number, like an ID number, so that a sentence “about formulas” became a sentence “about numbers.” Arithmetic began to talk about itself. Then he wrote a sentence that says, roughly: this sentence cannot be proved in this system. Think about it. If the system managed to prove it, the sentence would be saying something false, and the system would contain a contradiction. So if the system is consistent, the sentence truly cannot be proved. Of course this is only to help the imagination; the rigorous version is more delicate.
Spiritual meaning: say it accurately first

Those of us who share the gospel need to be especially careful. Some brother excitedly tells a friend: “Mathematics has proved that human reason is useless, so you should believe in Jesus!” If that friend works in science or engineering, he will smile politely and then never talk with you about faith again as long as he lives. Peter says to be ready with an answer, and to give it with gentleness and fear of God. Saying it accurately is itself a kind of gentleness.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear. (1 Peter 3:15)
2. Three versions that get it wrong
It cannot prove God, and it cannot deny God

The first wrong version: Gödel proved that God exists. The word God does not appear in the theorems; they are about formal systems. The second wrong version: Gödel proved that nothing is certain and truth is relative. Friends, how can a rigorously proved theorem prove that nothing is certain? Then it would be uncertain itself. And a statement that cannot be proved in system A can often be proved in a stronger system B. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy takes particular care to explain that the theorems do not mean some truths are unprovable in an absolute sense.

The third wrong version: every system is incomplete. In fact Presburger arithmetic, which has only addition, and Tarski’s theory of Euclidean geometry are both complete. They do not meet the conditions, so the theorems have no hold on them. So I want to say the title “truth is bigger than proof” carefully: no single fixed axiom system can capture all the truths of arithmetic. The Swedish mathematician Franzén wrote an entire book devoted to clearing up its uses and abuses. The title is a fun one: An Incomplete Guide.

This is not just a word game for logicians. Mathematics really does contain such examples. Goodstein’s theorem was proved in 1944, but in 1982 Kirby and Paris showed that it cannot be proved in Peano arithmetic, the standard system, and that stronger tools are needed. The continuum hypothesis is the same: Cohen showed in the 1960s that it is independent of the standard axioms of set theory. These are boundaries that mathematicians honestly walked up to.

There is also a deeper debate. Two scholars, Lucas and Penrose, argued that people can see that the Gödel sentence is true while a machine system cannot, so the human mind is not a machine. The idea is attractive, especially to us Christians. But I must tell you honestly: the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy points out that the field generally regards these arguments as having failed. The reason is that we know the sentence is true only on the assumption that the system is consistent, and people cannot always see whether a system is consistent. We should not pretend not to see the holes in an argument just because it favors us.
Spiritual meaning: having limits does not mean being useless

So was Gödel himself pessimistic? Not at all. He was a rational optimist who believed that many problems would eventually be solved. After the theorem was published, mathematics did not close its doors. It only grew deeper. This is just the posture Christians should take toward reason. Jesus wants us to love God with all our mind, and the mind is His gift. At the same time, Proverbs reminds us:
Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight. (Proverbs 3:5-6)

“Don’t lean on your own understanding” does not mean “you are forbidden to use your understanding.” It is like driving with a GPS: you should use it, but it cannot replace knowing the road yourself. Use it, but do not worship it.
3. The logician who believed in God
Do not say more on his behalf

So did Gödel believe in God? We must be very precise here. He was baptized as a Lutheran but belonged to no church. He described his belief as theism, following Leibniz rather than Spinoza, and he believed in an afterlife. His wife Adele said he often read the Bible in bed on Sunday mornings. He also wrote, roughly, that most religions are bad but religion itself is not. Friends, this was a man of conviction, but we cannot call him an evangelical brother. Let us not say more on his behalf.

He also left a manuscript that argues in modal logic for the existence of God. The earliest version dates to around 1941, and in 1970, thinking he was about to die, he gave it to the scholar Dana Scott. But he would not publish it, reportedly out of fear that people would think he really believed in God. You see, even someone like him feared what others would think. In 2013 two computer scientists used automated theorem provers to verify the proof, and some reports ran headlines like “Computer proves God exists.” But they themselves said plainly that a computer can only check whether the reasoning is valid, and that discussion of the concepts and axioms remains a human responsibility. Sobel also pointed out that these axioms lead to everything true becoming necessary. Valid logic does not mean the premises are true.

His later years make me sad. For a long time he feared being poisoned and would eat only food his wife prepared. At the end of 1977 his wife was hospitalized, and he refused to eat. On January 14, 1978, he died in Princeton. The death certificate gave starvation and exhaustion, caused by a personality disorder. I mention this not out of curiosity. One of the most capable reasoning minds in the world also needed to be cared for. Mental illness is not a sin, and it does not mean you are not smart enough or your faith is too small. If you or a family member are living in this kind of fear, please seek professional help. Gödel’s good friend Einstein often walked home together with him. Sometimes a person willing to walk beside you saves more than a proof.

Pilate once asked Jesus, “What is truth?” and then walked out without waiting for the answer. What a pity, for the answer was standing right in front of him. Only hours earlier Jesus had said to His disciples:
Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me. (John 14:6)

This is a sentence that no axiom system can hold. Please note, I am not saying that faith needs no reasons. The disciples saw the risen Jesus with their own eyes, and our faith rests on that testimony, which can be examined. But knowing a person is different from proving a theorem. Before you marry, you can look at a lot of evidence and learn that the other person is trustworthy, but in the end you still have to stand there and say: I will.
Spiritual meaning: the foolishness of God

God did not put salvation inside a proof that only geniuses can understand. If He had, I would be the first one left out today. He let His beloved Son be nailed to a cross, and raised Him from the dead, so that the grandmother selling vegetables at the market and the young person studying for a doctorate come to Him in the very same way. Paul calls this the foolishness of God.
because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men. (1 Corinthians 1:25)

Brothers and sisters, today we learned three things. First, cite accurately. The Bible is my standard, and truth does not need padding. Second, reason has limits, but it is not useless. Humility overcomes pride, and it overcomes laziness too. Third, truth is in the end a person: life first, then relationship, and even knowing the truth works this way. Let God be God and people be people.

This week please do one thing: look up one claim you often repeat, either “science proves faith” or “science refutes faith,” find the original source, and see what it actually said. If you have a friend who does not yet believe, you can ask lightly: is the thing you are most sure of in life something you can prove? And then listen to him.

Let us pray together: God of wisdom, thank You for giving me a mind that can think, and thank You for letting me run into its limits. Forgive my pride, and forgive my laziness. Thank You, Lord Jesus, that You are the truth, that You died for me and rose again. Help me to love You with all my mind, and to trust You with all my heart. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. What have you heard in the past about Gödel, or about other scientists, that you now find needs correcting? How do you usually check such things?
2. Which side are you more likely to fall into: handing all of faith over to logic, or using faith as an excuse not to think?
3. Gödel’s story reminds us that even the smartest people need company. Who around you needs someone to walk a stretch of the road with them right now?
